title: Charge
subtitle: A dangerous line. A deliberate sidestep. An opening to strike.
summary: The boss commits to a fast movement and uses its body as the weapon. In this variant, it can aim before locking on, but cannot turn once the direction is fixed.
learning: Read the commitment, move fully out of the lane, and use the recovery window.

demo.title: Watch the commitment
demo.intro: Compare two responses to the same attack. Scrub the timeline to inspect each phase.
phaseDescriptions: The boss can still adjust its aim. An early sidestep may be tracked.
Direction is now fixed. Move sideways until your whole body clears the lane.
The boss rushes along the fixed line. Distance alone will not protect you.
The boss has stopped and is recovering. This is the opening for a counterattack.
demo.reducedMotion: Animation starts paused. Use the phase buttons or timeline to explore without playback.
demo.diagramDescription: Top-down diagram of an armored boss charging toward a creature. A sideways dodge clears the lane; running along the lane leads to a hit.
demo.overlayNote: The colored lane explains the mechanic. A real game may telegraph it through pose, sound, or effects.

steps.title: Wait for the commitment
steps.body: Look for the pose, sound, or aiming cue that says the direction is fixed. Until then, the boss may still turn toward you.

steps.title: Move across the line
steps.body: Move perpendicular to the charge. Your whole collision shape must leave the danger lane; a small sideways shift may not be enough.

steps.title: Punish the miss
steps.body: After the boss stops, move into range and attack. Finish your response before the next action begins.

mistakes.title: Running along the lane
mistakes.body: You gain distance but remain in the path of the attack. A faster boss can still catch you.

mistakes.title: Dodging too early
mistakes.body: Before commitment, the boss may adjust its aim and follow your movement.

designNotes.title: Make commitment visible
designNotes.body: Separate tracking from commitment with a readable cue. The player needs to know when the rule changes.

designNotes.title: Leave a reachable escape
designNotes.body: Allow enough time for ordinary movement to clear the lane from intended starting positions. This example requires no dash, jump, or invulnerability.

designNotes.title: Give recovery a purpose
designNotes.body: The opening must cover travel back into attack range as well as the counterattack itself. Extra damage should still make progress faster.

story.title: A defender at the floodgate
story.body: For example, a human gatekeeper drives an armored ram at a canal crossing. Their job is to keep the creature away from the settlement beyond the gate. A narrow crossing, a heavy vehicle, and a costly turn make the charge belong to this place.

adaptation.title: Protection with a readable condition
adaptation.body: The front plow could block frontal projectiles while it is lowered during the charge, then lift during recovery. Show the block with a distinct impact effect; keep side or recovery hits useful. Tune the lane and recovery against the movement and range available at this point in progression. Do not silently erase upgrades or invent an immunity when a hit lands.

distinction.title: Charge ≠ dash ≠ lunge
distinction.body: A charge threatens a lane through committed body movement. A dash can simply reposition the boss. A lunge is usually a short closing strike. This page covers one charge variant, not a universal rule for every game.

quiz.question: The direction is fixed. What is the reliable escape in this example?
options: Run straight away from the boss.
Move sideways until your whole body leaves the lane.
Stand still and wait for recovery.
quiz.explanation: Move across the line. After the direction locks, the boss cannot follow that sideways movement. Distance along the same line does not remove the collision risk.
